title: Weight tracks fuel economy best, r = −0.83

title: Driving fell for one year in the 1973 oil shock, two in the 1979 shock and five from 2006

title: Beak depth falls with beak length across all penguins but rises within every species
subtitle: Paper-mode figure: no title block or footer; the claim is the caption's first sentence
form: three-panel figure: scatter with fits, dot plot with means, interval plot
data: Palmer penguins, Gorman, Williams and Fraser (2014), 342 birds with complete measurements
caption: Beak depth falls with beak length across all penguins but rises within every species. a, Beak length against beak depth for 342 penguins; the grey line is the least-squares fit to all birds (r = −0.24), the coloured lines are fits within each species (r = 0.39, 0.65 and 0.64 for Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo). b, Beak depth by species and sex; small dots are birds, ringed dots are means. Gentoo beaks are 3.4 to 3.5 mm shallower than those of the other species of the same sex, and males are deeper than females by 1.5 to 1.7 mm in every species, so the differences between species, not the relation within them, make the pooled slope negative. c, Pearson r between beak length and depth with 95 % intervals from Fisher's z: the sign turns positive once species is taken into account (r = 0.53) and stays positive within species and sex (r = 0.19). n = 342 birds with complete measurements, 333 with recorded sex (b and the last row of c). Data: Palmer penguins, Gorman, Williams and Fraser (2014), PLoS ONE 9(3): e90081; Palmer Station LTER; via the palmerpenguins R package and vega-datasets 2.8.0; figure drawn by examples/python/science/journal_penguins.py at git 4c16514.
alt: Three panels. a: beak depth against beak length; the pooled fit slopes down (r = −0.24) while each species' fit slopes up. b: Gentoo beaks are about 3.4 mm shallower than Adelie and Chinstrap in both sexes. c: correlations with intervals, negative pooled and positive within species (0.53).

alt: Slope chart of life expectancy in 1950 and 2023 for twelve countries. All rise. Egypt rises most, from 34 to 72 years; United States least, from 68 to 79.

title: Life expectancy rose in all 236 countries since 1950, but the trend hides collapses
subtitle: Life expectancy at birth · one country per panel, the other 235 countries and territories in grey · each loss from the year before the crisis
data: Our World in Data, period life expectancy at birth (UN WPP 2024 and others), 1950–2023, countries only
alt: Six small line charts of life expectancy from 1950 to 2023 over all other countries in grey: Japan gained 25 years, steadily (1950: 59 years · no fall above 0.5 in a year); China lost 15 years to famine (1960: 33 years); Lebanon lost 30 years to civil war (1976: 36 years); Rwanda lost 31 years to genocide (1994: 12 years); Eswatini lost 18 years to HIV (2004: 44 years, peak 62 in 1988); Bolivia lost 6 years to covid-19 (2021: 61 years).

title: Jean Valjean shares a chapter with 36 of the other 76 characters, more than anyone
subtitle: Co-occurrence network of Les Misérables, 77 characters and 254 links, force layout
data: Knuth, The Stanford GraphBase (1993), Les Misérables co-occurrences, via vega-datasets 2.8.0
alt: Two network drawings of the 77 characters of Les Misérables. Left: nodes coloured by the six largest of 11 groups. Right: Jean Valjean and his 36 neighbours highlighted in terracotta; they span 7 of the 11 groups. The next best connected character, Gavroche, has 22 neighbours.

title: Valjean co-appears 158 times with other characters, 1.5 times as often as Marius
subtitle: Les Misérables · the 50 most connected of 77 characters · the area of each name is proportional to its co-appearances
data: Knuth, The Stanford GraphBase (1993), Les Misérables co-occurrences, via vega-datasets 2.8.0
alt: Word cloud of the 50 most connected of the 77 characters of Les Misérables, word area proportional to co-appearances. Largest: Valjean (158), Marius (104), Enjolras (91), Courfeyrac (84), Cosette (68), Combeferre (68). Valjean has 1.5 times the co-appearances of Marius, and shares a chapter with 36 characters.
note: Layout: deterministic Archimedean spiral, largest word first, collision-checked on the rendered text boxes; no random seed involved.

title: Humans and chimpanzees split 6.5 million years ago, about a tenth of primate history
subtitle: Time-scaled phylogeny of 12 primates; approximate divergence times, illustrative; after TimeTree (Kumar et al. 2022)
data: Approximate divergence times after TimeTree 5 (Kumar et al. 2022), rounded; illustrative
alt: A rectangular phylogeny of 12 primates with time running from 70 million years ago on the left to the present on the right. Great apes in teal, Old World monkeys in terracotta, New World monkeys in indigo. Humans and chimpanzees split 6.5 million years ago, 9% of the 70 million years since the first split of the primates.
note: Illustrative: the topology is standard but the divergence times are rounded approximations after TimeTree, typed into the script. 6.5 / 70 = 0.093.

title: Two thirds of US petroleum moves vehicles, and exports now exceed imports
subtitle: Petroleum in 2025, million barrels a day: sources, products and the sectors that use them · 13.9 of 20.7 (67 %) to transportation
data: EIA Monthly Energy Review, petroleum supply and consumption by product and sector, 2025
alt: Sankey diagram of US petroleum in 2025, million barrels a day. Supply of 31.7: crude oil from US fields 13.7, natural gas liquids 7.5, imports 7.9, biofuels 1.4, processing gain 1.0. Exports take 10.8; 20.7 is supplied: motor gasoline 8.9, jet fuel 1.7, distillate 3.9, residual fuel 0.3, gas liquids 3.9, other products 1.9. Transportation uses 13.9 (67 %), industry 5.7, homes 0.59, commerce 0.48, power plants 0.09.
note: Products supplied is EIA's measure of consumption. Gas liquids include the ethane and other feedstocks the petrochemical industry uses; outside industry they are propane. Motor gasoline includes the ethanol blended into it, which is why biofuels enter on the supply side.

title: Dogs and wolves split 14,900 years ago; the first dogs numbered about 2,000
subtitle: Tube width: effective population size, from a coalescent model of seven canid genomes · arrows: gene flow
form: population tree with tube widths (demographic history)
data: Freedman et al. (2014), PLOS Genetics, G-PhoCS estimates, Table S12
alt: Population tree of dogs, wolves and the golden jackal, tube widths proportional to effective population size. The golden jackal splits from the ancestor of dogs and wolves 398,000 years ago. That ancestor, 44,993 strong, splits into dogs and wolves 14,874 years ago. The first dogs number about 1,999; the Dingo splits off 12,795 years ago and Boxer and Basenji 12,102 years ago. Wolves split about 13,455 years ago into lineages of 5,426 (Chinese), 26,092 (Israeli) and 11,427 (Croatian). Gene flow: Israeli wolf to Basenji 18 %, Basenji to Israeli wolf 7 %, between Chinese wolf and Dingo 3–4 %, from the dog-wolf ancestor into the golden jackal 99 %.
note: Calibrated with μ = 1 × 10⁻⁸ per site per generation and three-year generations, as in the paper; the mutation rate is the main source of uncertainty in the dates. Total migration rates are probabilities over the whole band and can exceed 100 %; the arrows are placed at an arbitrary time within the band. The two wolf splits, 13,455 and 13,389 years ago, are within each other's intervals.
